warmup.q: The payments program is written in Java. It starts in a container limited to 1 GB of memory and 1.5 CPUs (one and a half processors' worth of time), on a computer with 8 GB and 12 CPUs. Nobody tells Java how much memory to use. On JDK 25, what does it choose?
options: 2 GB for its objects (a quarter of the computer's 8 GB) and 12 CPUs, because Java sees the whole computer
256 MB for its objects (a quarter of the 1 GB limit) and 2 CPUs, because Java reads the container's limits
1 GB for its objects and 1 CPU, exactly the container's limits
768 MB for its objects (three quarters of the limit) and 12 CPUs
warmup.why: Java reads the container's limit files when it starts. memory.max says 1 GB, and by default Java keeps a quarter of that for its objects: 256 MB. cpu.max says 150 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms, which it rounds up to 2 CPUs. With that little, it also picks its simplest garbage collector, Serial (the garbage collector is the part of Java that frees memory nobody uses). The lab box printed exactly that. The first option is what Java does when it fails to see the container, a real bug that the last section meets.

sections.h: Looking from outside: a container is a process on a shared kernel
sections.html:
Let's start a container and look at it from both sides. Docker is a free program that runs containers. On a Mac, it runs them all inside one Linux virtual machine (VM), a pretend computer with its own operating system, which this track calls the Docker VM. Start a container that runs sleep, a program that waits and does nothing. Inside it, ps, the command that lists processes, shows sleep as PID 1. (A PID is a process's number, and a process is a running program.) From the host's side, the Docker VM that runs every container, the same process is PID 40037. Its status file says NSpid: 40037 1, one number for each side. And uname -r, which prints the version of the kernel (the core of the operating system), says 6.12.76-linuxkit in both places. There's no second kernel, and nothing started up from scratch. A container is a process.

The problem containers solve is old: run many programs on one computer so that each acts as if it were alone. The payments program shouldn't see the nightly job's processes, files or network ports (the numbers that say which program a network message is for). A memory leak in one shouldn't get the other killed. And a program that an attacker breaks into shouldn't be able to change the computer's clock or add code to the kernel.

The simplest complete answer is a virtual machine for each program, with its own kernel on pretend hardware. That keeps almost everything apart, and it costs a kernel, a start-up and a slice of memory set aside for every program.

Containers keep one kernel and use four things it already has. Namespaces give a process its own view of the system: its own PID numbers, hostname (the computer's name), network devices and view of which disks are attached where. A cgroup caps how much it can use: tasks (processes and threads), memory, CPU time. Capabilities and seccomp limit what it may ask the kernel to do. And an overlay gives it its own files, laid over a shared, read-only image, the set of files a container starts from. Each one is an ordinary kernel feature that works without Docker, and this lesson uses them that way.

A block of flats is a good picture. Namespaces are the walls and the private letterbox: a tenant sees only their own rooms and their own post, and can number their door 1. The cgroup is the meter: so much water and power, and the fuse trips for this flat only. Capabilities and seccomp are the house rules: you may hang pictures, but not touch the boiler. The overlay is a furnished flat: the furniture belongs to the building, and what you change is yours until you move out.

The figure is the picture for the whole lesson. One kernel serves everything, and a container is a few processes wrapped in those four layers. Everything in this track so far still holds inside a container, because there's only one of each part. The scheduler that picks what runs is the same one. So are the page cache, which keeps file data in memory, and the OOM killer, which ends a process when memory runs out.

That's also where the flats picture breaks. Real flats share foundations, but each has its own wiring. Every container shares the one kernel, so a kernel bug that one container can reach is a bug in every container on the machine. That's why Docker's seccomp filter blocks dozens of system calls (What a kernel does: system calls and user mode), io_uring among them. Next, we'll take the first layer apart: what a namespace hides.

try.title: Find a container's process from the host
steps: Run this on your Mac, from the labs folder. It starts a container that sleeps, asks Docker for its process's PID on the host, and looks at that process from a second container that shares the host's list of processes (--pid=host).
Predict the PID ps shows inside, and the NSpid line outside. The last line removes the container.

code.title: on your Mac, in the labs folder
code.html: docker run -d --name sfz-os12-ledger --hostname ledger sfz-labbox:1 sleep 300 > /dev/null docker exec sfz-os12-ledger ps -o pid,ppid,comm pid=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' sfz-os12-ledger); echo "host PID: $pid" docker run --rm --pid=host --cap-add SYS_PTRACE sfz-labbox:1 bash -c " ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p $pid grep NSpid /proc/$pid/status readlink /proc/$pid/ns/pid /proc/$pid/ns/net /proc/$pid/ns/user /proc/1/ns/pid /proc/1/ns/net /proc/1/ns/user uname -r" docker exec sfz-os12-ledger uname -r docker rm -f sfz-os12-ledger > /dev/null

try.expect:
PIDs and namespace numbers differ on your machine:

  PID  PPID COMMAND
    1     0 sleep
    7     0 ps
host PID: 40037
  PID  PPID COMMAND
40037 40008 sleep
NSpid:	40037	1
pid:[4026532698]
net:[4026532700]
user:[4026531837]
pid:[4026531836]
net:[4026531840]
user:[4026531837]
6.12.76-linuxkit
6.12.76-linuxkit

Inside, sleep is PID 1. The host knows it as 40037, a child of the process Docker uses to start containers, and NSpid lists both numbers, outermost first. Its PID and network namespaces have different numbers from the host's. (/proc/1 in a --pid=host container is the VM's own first process.) Its user namespace is the same one: Docker doesn't use user namespaces by default, so root, the administrator, in the container is root to the kernel. The kernel version is identical inside and out.

aside.title: Then why does Docker on a Mac need a virtual machine at all?
aside.html: Containers share the kernel they run on, and they need a Linux kernel, because namespaces and cgroups are Linux features. macOS has a different kernel without them. So Docker Desktop starts one small Linux virtual machine and runs every container inside it, all sharing that VM's kernel. On a Linux computer there's no VM in between: containers run on the computer's own kernel.

video.title: A container is a process on a shared kernel

sections.h: Namespaces: what a process can see
sections.html:
In the privileged lab box, unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --net --ipc bash starts a shell that can set its hostname to ledger-box, while the box keeps the name box-priv. (The privileged box is the lab box with its safety filters off, and a shell is the program that runs the commands you type.) Inside, ps -e lists two processes, with bash as PID 1. ip link, which lists network devices, finds only a loopback device, the one a computer uses to talk to itself, switched off. There's no eth0, the usual network device, at all.

The kernel keeps many tables that used to be shared by every process. There's the list of PIDs and the hostname. There are the network devices, with their addresses, ports and routes. And there's the list of mounted file systems. A namespace is a separate copy of one of those tables. Every process belongs to exactly one namespace of each kind, and /proc/<pid>/ns/ shows them as numbers such as pid:[4026532834]. (/proc is a folder the kernel fills with live facts about each process.) A child process starts in its parent's namespaces. unshare, or the system call clone with flags such as CLONE_NEWPID, puts a process into new ones. setns joins existing ones, which is how docker exec gets a shell into a running container. Linux has eight kinds:

namespace gives the process its own in a container
pid process numbers the app is PID 1
mnt list of mounted file systems (which disks are attached where) its own root folder
net network devices, addresses, ports, routes its own eth0 and localhost
uts hostname the container ID as hostname
ipc shared memory and message queues between processes no shared memory with neighbours
user mapping of user and group IDs root inside, nobody outside (off in Docker by default)
cgroup view of the cgroup tree (the next section) its own cgroup looks like /
time offsets for some of its clocks rarely used

The PID namespace has two effects you met in Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals. Its first process is PID 1, and it takes on the jobs of init, the first process of a whole system. It must reap orphans, collecting the exit status of children whose parents have died. And the kernel delivers it only the signals it has set up code to handle, apart from SIGKILL sent from outside. (A signal is a short message from the kernel to a process, and SIGKILL is the one that ends it at once.) When that PID 1 exits, the kernel kills every other process in the namespace. Nested namespaces give a process one PID for each level, which is the NSpid line.

In the flats, each kind of namespace is one more private thing: your own door numbers, your own letterbox, your own name on the bell.

Namespaces only change answers. A process in its own PID namespace sees 2 processes instead of 300. It can still make new processes until the machine's task table is full, or take memory until the computer runs out. That's the opening's nightly job. Its copies had small numbers in their own namespace, and they used up the one task table that every container shares.

Seeing less isn't using less. A namespace hides; it doesn't limit.

Next, we'll meet the layer that does limit.

try.title: Make namespaces with unshare
steps: Making namespaces needs the privileged box: from the labs folder, docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv. (Docker's seccomp filter blocks unshare in the everyday box, as What a kernel does: system calls and user mode showed.)
The block prints the shell's hostname and namespace numbers, starts a shell in new PID, mount, UTS, network and IPC namespaces, and looks around. Predict which lines differ.

code.title: in the privileged lab box
code.html: echo "outside: $(hostname), $(readlink /proc/self/ns/pid /proc/self/ns/uts /proc/self/ns/net | tr '\n' ' ')" unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --net --ipc bash -c ' hostname ledger-box echo "inside: $(hostname), $(readlink /proc/self/ns/pid /proc/self/ns/uts /proc/self/ns/net | tr "\n" " ")" ps -e ip -brief link show lo ip -brief link show eth0' echo "outside again: $(hostname)"

try.expect:
Namespace numbers differ:

outside: box-priv, pid:[4026532698] uts:[4026532696] net:[4026532700] 
inside: ledger-box, pid:[4026532834] uts:[4026532832] net:[4026532835] 
  PID TTY          TIME CMD
    1 ?        00:00:00 bash
    7 ?        00:00:00 ps
lo               DOWN           00:00:00:00:00:00 <LOOPBACK> 
outside again: box-priv
Device "eth0" does not exist.

Every namespace number changed, the hostname changed only inside, and the new PID namespace holds two processes, numbered from 1. --mount-proc mounted a fresh /proc for that namespace, which is why ps sees nothing else. The new network namespace has only a loopback device, switched off, and eth0 doesn't exist there. (The error line comes out last because it goes to a separate channel for errors.) Back outside, the hostname is untouched.

sections.h: Cgroups: how much a process can use
sections.html:
Take the same kind of shell, move it into a cgroup with pids.max set to 20 and memory.max to 64M, and it stops twice. forks.c, a small C program that keeps making child processes, gets 19 children, and then prints fork number 20 failed: EAGAIN. hog.c, which keeps taking memory, holds 48 MB, and asking for 16 MB more gets it killed with exit code 137.

A cgroup (control group) is a set of processes that the kernel counts and limits together. This track has already used three of its limits: pids.max for tasks, cpu.max for CPU time and memory.max for memory. In cgroup v2, the current version and the default on today's Linux systems and in the lab box, the groups form one tree of folders under /sys/fs/cgroup. Making a group is mkdir, making a folder. Every process is in exactly one group, listed in that group's file cgroup.procs, and writing a PID into that file moves the process there. A group's limits apply to everything below it, so a limit on a parent also caps every group under it.

Each kind of resource has a controller, the part of the kernel that counts it, and each controller has files:

controller limit how much now what happened
pids pids.max pids.current pids.events: max
memory memory.max, memory.high memory.current, memory.stat memory.events: max, oom, oom_kill
cpu cpu.max, cpu.weight cpu.stat cpu.stat: nr_throttled

Limits act at the moment the resource is spent. A fork or clone that would pass pids.max fails with EAGAIN, and threads count, because each thread (a line of work inside a process) is a task. When a process first touches new memory, the kernel must find it a page (a 4 KB piece of memory), and that's a page fault. If the page would push memory.current past memory.max, the kernel first tries to reclaim memory inside the group, by dropping copies of file data it can read again. If that fails, it runs the OOM killer on the group's biggest process. That ends in SIGKILL, and exit code 137 is 128 plus 9, the number of SIGKILL. A group that has used up its cpu.max budget is throttled, made to wait, until the next period. docker run --pids-limit 20 --memory 64m --cpus 0.5 writes exactly these files. So does Kubernetes, a system that runs containers across many computers, from the limits in its settings.

In the flats, the cgroup is the fuse box. It doesn't care what the tenant can see. It counts what they use, and trips for their flat alone. With a pids.max on the opening's nightly job, its copies would have hit the job's own limit, and the payments program would never have noticed.

Every container needs limits. Without them, the neighbours share its mistakes.

One rule shows up when you build a group by hand. In cgroup v2, a group that hands controllers down to its child groups, through cgroup.subtree_control, can't hold processes itself. That's why the Try it moves the box's processes into a child called init before it creates ledger. The stepper builds a whole container this way and runs it into both limits. Next, we'll see what stops a container's root user from asking the kernel for more power.

try.title: A fork bomb and a memory hog in a cgroup you made
steps: In the privileged box again. The block makes the cgroup ledger with pids.max 20, memory.max 64M and no swap. Then it runs os/c/l12/forks.c and os/c/l12/hog.c in it, each from a shell that first writes its own PID into cgroup.procs.
Predict the fork number that fails, the last "holding" line, and the exit code. The cgroup disappears when the box exits.

code.title: in the privileged lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/forks os/c/l12/forks.c && gcc -O2 -o /tmp/hog os/c/l12/hog.c cd /sys/fs/cgroup mkdir init; for p in $(cat cgroup.procs); do echo $p > init/cgroup.procs 2>/dev/null; done echo "+pids +memory +cpu" > cgroup.subtree_control mkdir ledger echo 20 > ledger/pids.max; echo 64M > ledger/memory.max; echo 0 > ledger/memory.swap.max cat ledger/pids.max ledger/memory.max bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/ledger/cgroup.procs; cat /proc/self/cgroup; /tmp/forks 500' cat ledger/pids.events bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/ledger/cgroup.procs; /tmp/hog 256; echo "exit code $?"' grep -E '^(max|oom|oom_kill) ' ledger/memory.events

bash -c ran forks as its last command, so forks replaced it in the same task: 1 plus 19 children is 20, and fork number 20 failed with EAGAIN, counted once in pids.events. hog reached 48 MB. Its next block would have taken the group past 64 MB, reclaim found nothing to free, and the OOM killer sent it SIGKILL: exit code 137 and oom_kill 1. max counts every time the group reached its limit and had to reclaim, not only the kills. The Killed line from bash arrives last because it's written to the error channel.

sections.h: Limiting root, and giving it files: capabilities, seccomp and an overlay
sections.html:
In the lab box, root, the administrator account, can change a file's owner with chown. But date -s 2030-01-01, which sets the clock, fails with cannot set date: Operation not permitted. Start the container with --cap-drop CHOWN, and chown fails the same way, still as root.

Without a user namespace, which Docker doesn't use by default, root in a container is user 0 to the kernel, the same user as root on the host. What holds it back is that Linux doesn't ask "is this user 0?" before a powerful operation. It splits root's power into about 40 capabilities, each guarding one group of operations. CAP_CHOWN covers changing file owners, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE using ports below 1024, CAP_SYS_TIME setting the clock, and CAP_SYS_ADMIN mounting file systems and much more. A process holds a set of them, and the kernel checks the one each operation needs. Docker gives a container 14 and drops the rest. So the CapEff mask in /proc/self/status, a number with one bit per capability, decodes to cap_chown, cap_kill, cap_net_bind_service and 11 others, and no cap_sys_time. --privileged gives all of them and switches seccomp off; that's the box-priv this lesson has used for its experiments.

seccomp is the filter from What a kernel does: system calls and user mode. It runs before every system call, and Docker's default list refuses about 44 of them, including mount, unshare and the io_uring calls. The two work at different levels. Capabilities say which powerful operations a process may perform. seccomp takes whole system calls out of reach, in case the kernel has a bug in one of them. In the flats, capabilities are the house rules, and seccomp is the locked door to the boiler room.

Last, the files. An image is a stack of read-only layers, and sfz-labbox:1 has 7 of them. A container's root folder is an overlay mount: the image layers below, as lowerdir, and an empty, writable upperdir of its own on top. A read finds the file in the highest layer that has it. The first write to a file from a lower layer copies the whole file up into the upper folder and changes the copy. That's copy-on-write again (Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer), per file instead of per page. A delete writes a marker, called a whiteout, that hides the lower file. docker diff lists the upper folder, and docker rm throws it away, so a container never changes its image. A hundred containers from one image share its layers, on disk and in the page cache. It's the furnished flat: the furniture stays with the building, and your changes leave with you.

A container never changes its image. Keep data that must last in a volume, a folder mounted from outside.

So a container is processes, namespaces, a cgroup, a few rules and an overlay. Next, we'll watch a program read its own cgroup to decide how big to be.

try.title: Capabilities, then the writable layer
steps: On your Mac, from the labs folder. The first command decodes the container's capabilities with capsh, then tries one allowed operation and one forbidden one. The second drops CHOWN.
The rest starts a container, changes one file from the image, deletes another and creates a third, then asks Docker what's in its upper layer. Predict the letters docker diff prints.

code.title: on your Mac, in the labs folder
code.html: docker run --rm sfz-labbox:1 bash -c 'grep CapEff /proc/self/status; capsh --decode=$(grep CapEff /proc/self/status | cut -f2); touch /tmp/x; chown nobody /tmp/x && echo "chown: ok"; date -s 2030-01-01 > /dev/null' docker run --rm --cap-drop CHOWN sfz-labbox:1 bash -c 'touch /tmp/x; chown nobody /tmp/x' docker run -d --name sfz-os12-diff sfz-labbox:1 sleep 120 > /dev/null docker exec sfz-os12-diff bash -c 'echo "ISSUER=acme-bank" >> /etc/environment; rm /etc/legal; echo ok > /tmp/settle.csv' docker diff sfz-os12-diff docker rm -f sfz-os12-diff > /dev/null

The image itself is unchanged, and the next container from it starts clean.

sections.h: How Java sizes itself from the container's limits, and how to check
sections.html:
Java is one program that reads those cgroup files to size itself. Under --memory 1g --cpus 1.5, JDK 25 chose a 256 MB heap, 2 CPUs and the Serial collector. The heap is the memory Java keeps for a program's objects, and the collector, or garbage collector (GC), is the part of Java that frees objects nobody uses. In the same container with container support turned off, it chose a 1,984 MB heap and the G1 collector. It sized itself for the Docker VM's 7.9 GB and 12 CPUs, in a container that gets killed at 1 GB.

At start-up, the JVM (the Java virtual machine, the program that runs Java code) finds its cgroup in /proc/self/cgroup and reads its files. The default maximum heap is 25% of memory.max, a share set by -XX:MaxRAMPercentage. The CPU count is cpu.max's quota divided by its period, rounded up, and capped by the CPUs the container may use at all. That number decides how many threads the JVM starts for collecting garbage, for compiling code while it runs, and for running work in parallel. The collector is G1 only on what the JVM calls a "server-class machine", at least 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; below that, it's Serial. A 256 MB container gets a 126 MB heap, about half, because HotSpot, the JVM most people run, keeps a floor under small heaps. java -XshowSettings:system -version prints what the JVM found, and -Xlog:os+container=debug prints how it found it.

When detection fails, you get the 1,984 MB heap, and that has happened to real programs. On Linux 6.12, the kernel stopped listing cpuset, the controller that pins a group to chosen CPUs, in /proc/cgroups. JDK builds such as 17.0.12 and 21.0.5 treated that as a required controller gone missing. The bug report, JDK-8346874, shows the JVM logging "One or more required controllers disabled at kernel level" and sizing the heap from the host's memory. An early JDK 25 build printed "System not containerized". JDK 25 has the fix (JDK-8347129). The lab box runs kernel 6.12, and its log says Detected optional cpuset controller entry. On JDK 17 or 21, run -XshowSettings:system in the real image on the real computers, and look for System not containerized.

Check what the JVM detected. Don't assume it saw the container.

The same files answer "why is this container slow?", and they're the last tool of this track. The USE method, from the performance engineer Brendan Gregg, checks every resource for utilization (how busy it is), saturation (how much work waits for it) and errors. In a container, each has a file. For CPU: usage_usec in cpu.stat for utilization, and nr_throttled and cpu.pressure for saturation. For memory: memory.current against memory.max, then memory.pressure, then oom_kill in memory.events. For tasks: pids.current, and max in pids.events.

The *.pressure files are PSI (pressure stall information): the share of time that tasks in the group waited for that resource. some counts the time when at least one task waited, and full the time when all of them did. Each comes as averages over 10, 60 and 300 seconds, and as a running total in microseconds. Two busy workers under --cpus 0.5 stalled for 6.2 s of 11. One warning: inside a container, /proc/pressure, free and /proc/meminfo describe the whole VM, and so does top. The cgroup files describe your container.

try.title: Read the limits the way the JVM does
steps: On your Mac, from the labs folder. The first loop starts two containers with different limits, and prints the cgroup files next to the heap, collector and CPU count the JVM chose. Then the JVM runs once more with container support switched off.

The second part runs two busy workers, with stress-ng, in a container with half a CPU for 11 seconds, and reads its CPU pressure and throttling counters. Predict the heap for each run, and roughly what share of the time the workers stalled.

code.title: on your Mac, in the labs folder
code.html: for limits in "--memory 1g --cpus 1.5" "--memory 4g --cpus 4"; do echo "== $limits" docker run --rm $limits sfz-labbox:1 bash -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E " (MaxHeapSize|UseSerialGC|UseG1GC) " java -XshowSettings:system -version 2>&1 | grep -E "Effective CPU|Memory Limit"' done echo "== --memory 1g --cpus 1.5, container support off" docker run --rm --memory 1g --cpus 1.5 sfz-labbox:1 bash -c 'java -XX:-UseContainerSupport -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E " (MaxHeapSize|UseG1GC) "' docker run --rm --cpus 0.5 sfz-labbox:1 bash -c ' stress-ng --cpu 2 --timeout 12s --quiet & sleep 11 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.pressure grep -E "nr_periods|nr_throttled" /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat wait'

1 GB and 1.5 CPUs gave a 256 MB heap, 2 CPUs (1.5 rounded up) and Serial; 4 GB and 4 CPUs gave 1 GB and G1. With -XX:-UseContainerSupport, the JVM sized itself from the VM's 7.9 GB: a heap twice the container's whole limit. In the last run, total=6195106 means tasks in the group waited 6.2 s for the CPU during the 11 s. nr_throttled shows the group ran out of its 50 ms budget in 120 of 126 periods. avg10 is still climbing, because it's an average over the last 10 seconds.

refs.title: JDK-8346874: Linux kernel version 6.12 and newer breaks JVM container support
PSI: Pressure Stall Information (Linux kernel documentation)

opening:
Picture the small company whose program records card payments for coffee shops. One computer runs two of its programs: the payments program, and a nightly job that adds up what each shop is owed. Each runs in its own container, a boxed-off space with its own name, files and list of running programs.

One night a bug makes the job copy itself, over and over. Minutes later the payments program fails too, in a container nobody touched: it can't start the threads, the parallel lines of work, that it needs.

It's easy to think a container is a small computer, with its own name, files and even process number 1. Underneath, both are ordinary processes on one kernel, and the job used up something they share.

In I/O models: blocking, epoll and io_uring, Docker refused io_uring because one kernel serves every container. In this lesson, we'll find a container from outside, build one by hand, run it into its limits, and read the files Java reads to size itself. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a nightly job that copied itself until the payments program, in the container next door, couldn't start a thread. Both were processes on one kernel, and only a pids.max on the job's cgroup could have kept the mistake to itself.

If you have Docker, run cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max inside any container. max means no limit, so a neighbour's mistake can reach you.

That ends the Operating systems track and the Foundations part of the course. Next, Part II, Data on one machine, opens with SQL: a database program, often run in a container like these, that keeps payments in tables. Why can a question that reads like plain English get a surprising answer?

compare.note: A namespace changes the answers the kernel gives: which PIDs exist, what the hostname is, which network devices there are. It never makes a call fail for using too much. A cgroup changes nothing a process can see, apart from its own cgroup files, and it makes calls fail or processes die when they use too much: fork returns EAGAIN, a page fault ends in SIGKILL, a busy thread gets throttled. A container needs both. The left side alone can still fork-bomb the host, and the right side alone sees, and can signal, every process on it.

steps.say: An image is a folder of files. Copy a few programs into one, with the shared libraries (code files a program loads when it starts) that ldd says they need. In the privileged box, on a scratch tmpfs, a file system that lives in memory:
steps.code: mkdir -p /c && mount -t tmpfs -o size=200m tmpfs /c mkdir -p /c/image/bin /c/image/proc /c/image/tmp cp /tmp/forks /tmp/hog /c/image/bin/ # built from os/c/l12/ for b in bash ls cat hostname ps; do cp $(command -v $b) /c/image/bin/; done for lib in $(ldd /c/image/bin/* 2>/dev/null | grep -o '/[^ ]*\.so[^ ]*' | sort -u); do mkdir -p /c/image$(dirname $lib); cp $lib /c/image$lib done du -sh /c/image # 8.3M /c/image

steps.say: Give it a writable layer. The overlay lays an empty upper folder over the read-only image, and writes go up there.
steps.code: mkdir -p /c/upper /c/work /c/root mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=/c/image,upperdir=/c/upper,workdir=/c/work /c/root

steps.say: Make the cgroup and set its limits. First move the box's own processes into a child group, because a group that enables controllers for its children can't hold processes.
steps.code: cd /sys/fs/cgroup mkdir init; for p in $(cat cgroup.procs); do echo $p > init/cgroup.procs 2>/dev/null; done echo "+pids +memory +cpu" > cgroup.subtree_control mkdir ledger echo 20 > ledger/pids.max; echo 64M > ledger/memory.max; echo 0 > ledger/memory.swap.max

steps.say: Join the cgroup, then let unshare start a shell in new namespaces, with the overlay as its root folder. env -i gives it an empty environment (the named settings, such as PATH, that a program starts with), as a container's first program would get.
steps.code: bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/ledger/cgroup.procs exec env -i PATH=/bin LC_ALL=C unshare --pid --fork --mount --uts --net --ipc --cgroup \ --root=/c/root --mount-proc bash -c "hostname ledger-box; ...; forks 500; hog 256"' &

steps.say: What the container printed, and what the host saw. Inside: PID 1, a root folder with four folders in it, a cgroup that looks like /, and both limits. Outside: each process with two PIDs, the events in the cgroup's files, and the container's one file in the upper layer.

lab.title: Model cgroups, PID namespaces and the JVM's view of them
steps: Read Containers.kt. Cgroup is a folder with limits and event counters, PidNamespace numbers its tasks from 1, Task holds one PID per namespace level, and Host is the one kernel. Making tasks, moving them, forkIntoNewPidNamespace and kill (with the PID 1 rule) are written for you.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All nine fail.

Write checkPids: walk cg.lineage(), the group and every group above it. The first group that one more task would take past pidsMax counts pidsEventsMax and throws SysError("EAGAIN", ...). fork and startThread already call it.

Write touch: charge the memory, then, for each group in the lineage that is over memoryMaxMb, count max and oom, and kill the biggest task in that group or the groups below it until it fits, counting oom_kill.
Write JvmView.availableProcessors and defaultGc. The tests compare all of it with the files and JVM settings captured in the privileged box.
hints: c.pidsCurrent + 1 > max is the check: the new task is the one that would pass the limit.
Pick the victim with c.allTasks().maxWith(compareBy<Task> { it.rssMb }.thenBy { it.hostPid }), so ties go to the newest task, and call kill(victim, ...), which also zeroes its memory.
"150000 100000".split(Regex("\\s+")) gives quota and period; Math.ceil(quota / period) turns 1.5 into 2. "max" as the quota means no limit.
Server-class means cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1792: 2 GB minus 256 MB of slack.

drill.title: A cgroup from memory
drill.prompt: As root on a Linux computer with cgroup v2, where /sys/fs/cgroup is the real top of the tree, write the commands that create a group named settle with at most 50 tasks, 256 MB of memory and no swap, and half a CPU. Then start java -jar settle.jar inside it. Last, write where you'd look to see whether it hit each limit.

answer.html: cd /sys/fs/cgroup # (in the privileged lab box, first move its processes into a child group, as the Try-it does) echo "+pids +memory +cpu" > cgroup.subtree_control # controllers for the children mkdir settle echo 50 > settle/pids.max echo 256M > settle/memory.max echo 0 > settle/memory.swap.max echo "50000 100000" > settle/cpu.max # 50 ms per 100 ms bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/settle/cgroup.procs; exec java -jar settle.jar' # did it hit them? cat settle/pids.events # max N: forks or threads refused with EAGAIN cat settle/memory.events # oom_kill N: processes the OOM killer took grep throttled settle/cpu.stat # nr_throttled: periods it ran out of budget cat settle/cpu.pressure settle/memory.pressure # how long tasks waited

recap: A container is ordinary processes on the one shared kernel: NSpid shows each one's PID inside and on the host, and uname -r is the same everywhere.
Namespaces (pid, mnt, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time) give a process its own view. They change what it sees, never how much it can use.

A cgroup is a folder under /sys/fs/cgroup. pids.max makes fork fail with EAGAIN, memory.max ends in reclaim and then the OOM killer inside the group, and cpu.max throttles. The *.events files and cpu.stat count each hit.

Root in a default Docker container is user 0 to the kernel, held back by 14 capabilities and a seccomp filter, and --privileged removes both. The root folder is an overlay: read-only image layers plus the container's own upper layer, where the first write copies a file up.

The JVM sizes its heap (25% of memory.max), its CPU count (quota divided by period, rounded up) and its collector (G1 only from 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB) from these files. Check with -XshowSettings:system, and read waiting from cpu.stat and the PSI *.pressure files.
The limit: every container shares one kernel, so a kernel bug, or any resource without a limit, reaches them all. For a hard security boundary, you need a virtual machine.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Containers are small virtual machines, so the nightly job's container can't affect the payments program's container next to it." Explain what a container really is, which parts of that claim hold, and which don't.
explain.answer: A container is a set of ordinary processes on the computer's one kernel. Namespaces give them their own view: their own PIDs, hostname, network devices and list of mounted file systems. So the nightly job can't see or signal the payments program's processes, or take its ports. A cgroup limits what they use: if the job has a memory limit, a leak ends in the OOM killer inside the job's cgroup, and the payments program isn't a candidate. The overlay gives the job its own files over a shared, read-only image. All of that holds. What doesn't hold is the virtual-machine part. There's no second kernel: both containers make system calls into the same one. Without user namespaces, root in the job is user 0 to that kernel, held back only by 14 capabilities and a seccomp filter, so a kernel bug that one container can reach affects both. Anything without a limit is shared too. A job with no pids.max can fill the computer's task table, one with no memory limit can push the whole computer out of memory, and CPU without cpu.max is shared by weight. And settings for the whole computer, such as kernel settings, the page cache and the disk's speed, belong to everyone. So set limits on every container, never run them privileged, and use a virtual machine or a sandbox when you need a security boundary.

deeper.html:
User namespaces close the biggest gap in a default container. With one, root inside maps to a powerless user ID outside, so even an escape lands as nobody. Podman's rootless mode (Podman is another program that runs containers) and Docker's userns-remap setting use them, and Kubernetes has been adding user namespace support. They're not the default yet in most places, because some images and shared folders expect real root.

Where one kernel is too little separation, sandboxes put something between the container and the host's kernel. gVisor answers system calls with a kernel of its own that runs as an ordinary program. Kata Containers and Firecracker run each container, or each small function, in a tiny virtual machine with its own kernel. Both trade start-up time and some speed for less shared kernel code that an attacker could reach.

Two more memory files are worth knowing. memory.high is a soft limit: above it, the kernel slows the group's memory requests and reclaims hard, but never calls the OOM killer, which gives a program a slow warning instead of a sudden death. memory.oom.group, set to 1, makes the OOM killer take every process in the group together, which suits a container whose processes are useless without each other.

The USE method has a classic first minute on a whole computer, from Brendan Gregg: uptime, dmesg | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 and top. Each tool in that list reads files this track has opened: /proc/stat, /proc/meminfo, the per-process /proc/<pid>/ folders and the network counters. In a container, check whether a tool reads the cgroup's files or the whole machine's before you trust what it says.
